acts.title: Text A · Where the year goes
text: Most people overestimate what they will get done in a day and underestimate what they will have achieved in a year. That single sentence explains more about wasted time than any diary app.

Think about it as a calculation. By this time next year you will have lived through about three hundred and sixty-five evenings. If you set aside two of them a week for one thing, you will have spent roughly a hundred and four evenings on it. That is more hours than most university courses contain.

Nobody plans to lose those evenings. They go one at a time, and this is the difficulty: at eight o’clock on a Tuesday you will not be choosing between a language and nothing. You will be choosing between a language and a screen, while tired.
In five years you will have made that choice about two and a half thousand times.

items.q: What is the writer’s main point?
o: Small regular amounts of time add up to far more than people expect

items.q: What does the writer say the real choice is at eight on a Tuesday?
o: Between the thing and a screen, while tired

acts.title: Text B · Two questions worth asking
text: Stephen Covey’s advice is usually reduced to a grid, which is a shame, because the useful part is a question: what is important but not urgent?

Almost everything that will still matter in ten years sits in that category. Your health will not send you a reminder. Nobody will ring to ask whether you have stayed in contact with the people you like. By the time those things become urgent, you will have lost the chance to do them cheaply.
The second question is smaller and more practical. In a year’s time, what will you wish you had started today? People answer it quickly and honestly, and then, in most cases, do nothing.
This time next year you will be doing something with your evenings. The only decision available is what.

items.s: Covey’s useful idea, according to the writer, is a question rather than a grid.
Things that are important but not urgent tend to announce themselves.
The writer says people find the second question hard to answer.
The writer says most people act on their answer.
The final point is that the evenings will be spent either way.

acts.title: Look again at the two texts
text: By this time next year you will have lived through about three hundred and sixty-five evenings.
You will have spent roughly a hundred and four evenings on it.
At eight o’clock on a Tuesday you will not be choosing between a language and nothing.
You will be choosing between a language and a screen, while tired.
By the time those things become urgent, you will have lost the chance.
This time next year you will be doing something with your evenings.

items.q: “By this time next year you will have lived through…” — what does this form describe?
o: Something completed before a future point
Something in progress at a future point

items.q: “This time next year you will be doing something…” — and this one?
o: Something in progress at a future point

items.q: Which phrase goes with the future perfect?

acts.title: Standing in the future and looking around
rule: Both of these forms ask you to imagine a moment in the future and then describe it. The future continuous looks around at that moment and says what is going on. The future perfect looks backwards from it and says what is already done.
points: will be + -ing. In progress at a stated future moment. This time tomorrow I’ll be flying.
will have + past participle. Completed before a stated future moment. By Friday I’ll have finished.
The time phrase does the work
The continuous takes at / this time. The perfect takes by / by the time.
will have been + -ing, for duration up to a future point. By June I’ll have been working here ten years.
Will you be using the car this evening? is softer than Are you going to use it — it asks about circumstances rather than intentions.
eg: This time tomorrow I’ll be sitting on a train.
In progress at that moment.
At eight o’clock you’ll be choosing between a language and a screen.
In progress.
By Friday I’ll have finished the report.
Complete before that point.
By this time next year you’ll have spent a hundred evenings on it.
Complete before that point.
By the time those things become urgent, you’ll have lost the chance.
by the time + present, then future perfect.
In June I’ll have been working here for ten years.
Duration up to a future point.
Don’t call at seven — we’ll be eating.
A very common everyday use.
Will you be using the car tonight?
Polite enquiry about arrangements.
By 2030 half of those jobs will have disappeared.
A prediction with a deadline.
I’ll have been on this course for a year by then.
Perfect continuous with a state-like verb phrase.
acts.careful: After by the time, use a present tense, not a future one: “By the time she arrives, I’ll have left.” Never “by the time she will arrive”.

acts.title: Choosing between the two, in three questions
steps: I start the report on Monday and it takes four days. Today is Sunday.
Two facts. Now pick a future moment.
1 · Every one of these sentences needs a stated future point.
Is the action finished by Friday, or still going on?
2 · This is the only question that matters.
Finished → BY Friday I will have finished the report.
3 · Finished takes by + will have + past participle.
Still going → ON Wednesday I will still be writing it.
4 · In progress takes at / on + will be + -ing.

items.q: Finished before the point: By ten o’clock I ___.
In progress at the point: At ten o’clock I ___ across France.
Which preposition goes with the future perfect?
By the time the train ___, we’ll have eaten.

use: By this time next year I’ll have…

write.q: Write about 180 words looking forward from a fixed point — this time next year, or the year you turn a particular age. Use the future perfect at least three times for what will be finished by then, and the future continuous at least twice for what will be going on. Add one future perfect continuous with a length of time.
plan: the moment you are standing at
what will be finished by then
what will still be going on
one thing you are not sure of
write.model:
By this time next year I will have finished the data course, assuming I do not lose two months to something I cannot foresee. I will also have paid off the last of the loan, which I have been carrying since 2019 and have stopped mentioning.

What will still be going on is everything slower. I will still be living in the same flat — the lease runs to 2028 and I am not going to argue with it. I will still be doing the Thursday classes, because I have been doing them for four years and they cost almost nothing.

By next spring I will have been working in this building for six years, which is longer than I have done anything since school.

The part I am not sure of is the job itself. By the time the reorganization is finished, I may not have the same one. I will probably still be here in some form. Probably is doing a lot of work in that sentence.
